purpose: Owner decision: model wider food supply before letting calibrated town residents drive the food-budget chain. Only about a quarter of release-3 towns can be fed from one day's local grain collection; real cities of that size drew grain from far beyond a day's walk.
evidence_status: A declared scenario, not an Earth fit. No Earth pool in this checkout carries grain production and a freight network, so nothing is fitted or tested here. Every coefficient is one the atlas already uses and cites: Diocletian's Price Edict freight ratios (sea 1 : river down 5 : river up 10 : road 28 per km), the seasonal travel network, and Duncan-Jones (1982) on road haulage eating a staple's whole value at about 270 road-km.
inputs: Release-3 towns and residents (headline sliding density; flat density as alternative), the final rural people of the release-3 people ledger, the published cereal potential per cell, and the atlas freight network (polity.trade.cost_network) for the four trade months, built on the release-3 towns and tracks.
grain_available: Per cell: 10% of cereal potential above the remaining rural people's needs (2,500 kcal a day), the collection fraction the published ledgers already use. A 33% extraction sensitivity is reported beside it and is not the headline.
transport_cost_in_grain: Moving grain over a path costing c road-km equivalents delivers the share max(0, 1 - c/270). Costs are averaged over the four trade months as delivered shares.
stage_1_hinterland: Each season every land cell sends a quarter of its annual available grain to the town it can reach most cheaply (the inbound market hinterland the trade model already uses), delivering 1 - c/270. Cells beyond 270 deliver nothing and keep their grain.
stage_2_between_towns: Towns whose hinterland delivers more than their residents eat export the excess; towns short of grain import. Shipment from A to B delivers 1 - c(A to B)/270 of what leaves A. Links are served cheapest first (highest delivered share), each link moving as much as the exporter still has and the importer still needs. This gives a feasible plan, not the optimum: a different order could feed slightly more.
no_reshipment: Imported grain is not re-exported; a town can be an exporter or an importer, not both.
outputs: Per town: need, hinterland grain delivered, exports, imports received, fed share, status (self-sufficient, fed with imports, short), cheapest and farthest supplier. World: residents fed, grain consumed by transport, unused excess. Shipment list for the map.
ledger: Grain is conserved: available = delivered to towns + consumed in transport + left in cells or unused at exporters. People are not moved by this step; town residents stay at their calibrated size and shortfalls are reported, not corrected.
not_modelled: Other foods, fish and livestock; prices and markets; shipping capacity; storage through the year; state grain fleets; reshipment hubs. Cereal potential is the published wheat/barley potential, not observed harvests.
publication: A Settlements map option showing supply status and the main grain shipments, per-town CSV, and a report. The default map changes only in its legend: the white centre will mean fed including imports, with locally fed towns distinguished.
next_step_not_in_this_plan: Whether supply-fed calibrated residents should replace the 7.5% request inside the blind-tested control chain remains a separate decision after these results.
review: Independent recomputation of hinterland delivery and the between-town plan with a separately written allocator; conservation checks; byte replay.
